fetched_contents.text: Invasive Trichoderma spp. infections: clinical presentation and outcome of cases from the literature and the FungiScope® registry Abstract Background Trichoderma spp. are filamentous fungi causing invasive fungal diseases in patients with haematological malignancies and in peritoneal dialysis patients. Objectives To analyse clinical presentation, predisposing factors, treatment and outcome of Trichoderma infections. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted for published cases of invasive Trichoderma infection in PubMed until December 2021 and by reviewing the included studies’ references. Cases from the FungiScope® registry were added to a combined analysis. Results We identified 50 invasive infections due to Trichoderma species, including 11 in the FungiScope® registry. The main underlying conditions were haematological malignancies in 19 and continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) in 10 cases. The most prevalent infection sites were lung (42%) and peritoneum (22%). Systemic antifungal therapy was administered in 42 cases (84%), mostly amphotericin B (n = 27, lipid-based formulation 13/27) and voriconazole in 15 cases (30%). Surgical interventions were performed in 13 cases (26%). Overall mortality was 48% (n = 24) and highest for allogeneic HSCT and solid organ transplantation (SOT) recipients [80% (4/5) and 77% (7/9), respectively]. In patients treated with amphotericin B, voriconazole and caspofungin, mortality was 55% (15/27), 46% (7/15) and 28% (2/7), respectively. Three out of four patients treated with a combination therapy of voriconazole and caspofungin survived. Conclusions Despite treatment with antifungal therapies and surgery, invasive Trichoderma infections are life-threatening complications in immunocompromised patients, especially after HSCT and SOT. In addition, Trichoderma spp. mainly affect the lungs in patients with haematological malignancies and the peritoneum in CAPD patients. Introduction Filamentous fungi, such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium and Trichoderma species, are found worldwide, commonly in soil and water habitats, and are known to produce mycotoxins.1 They can be found in rotten biological material, where they accelerate degradation of organic material.2Trichoderma is effective against common soil-borne pathogens and is thus used as a commercial biopesticide.3 As opposed to Aspergillus, Fusarium and Penicillium that cause severe infections in a broad variety of patients, Trichoderma has long been considered non-pathogenic in humans, but localized and disseminated infections in immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients have been reported worldwide.4Trichoderma longibrachiatum is the most commonly reported species associated with invasive fungal infections (IFI), followed by Trichoderma atroviride, Trichoderma bissettii, Trichoderma citrinoviride, Trichoderma harzianum, Trichoderma koningii, Trichoderma pseudokoningii and Trichoderma viride.5–7 Trichoderma species cause a variety of clinical manifestations, such as invasive pulmonary infection, peritonitis, CNS infection, endocarditis, fungaemia and disseminated disease affecting distant organs, especially in patients with haematological malignancies and those undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD).8–10 The tissue morphology of Trichoderma species is characterized by the presence of hyaline septate hyphae, similar to Aspergillus spp. and other agents of hyalohyphomycosis.4,11 Thus, culture and molecular approaches are necessary for diagnosis.4 Except for echinocandins and voriconazole, Trichoderma isolates show relatively high MICs in vitro of other antifungal drugs.12,13 The associated mortality rate is reported to be as high as 53%.14 Currently, there are no evidence-based guidelines for the clinical management of invasive Trichoderma infections. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive analysis from the FungiScope® registry and the literature to identify clinical presentation, predisposing factors, treatment, outcome and effective therapeutic options of invasive Trichoderma infections. Methods We collected cases from the medical literature (PubMed) and FungiScope®, a global registry for invasive fungal infections (IFI) (www.clinicaltrials.gov NCT 01731353).15 The PubMed database was searched for all reported cases of Trichoderma infections from database inception to 31 December 2021 using the search term (Trichoderma*) AND ((invasive OR disseminated OR infection) AND (case OR patient OR report)). References of articles were reviewed to identify additional studies (Figure 1). Authors of the studies were contacted to obtain further data. FungiScope® was approved by the local institutional review board and ethics committee of the University of Cologne, Germany (Study ID: 05-102). For each case, clinical data were collected: underlying conditions, symptoms and clinical signs, site(s) of infection, imaging findings, mycological evidence, antifungal treatment, antifungal susceptibility and clinical response and outcome. Mortality on days 42 and 90 after diagnosis of IFI and initiation of targeted therapy was documented. In addition, mortality attributed to the infection was noted. The follow-up period was defined as time from diagnosis of Trichoderma infection to last day of contact or death. Invasive Trichoderma infection was classified as proven or probable according to the revised criteria of the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer/Invasive Fungal Infections Cooperative Group and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Mycoses Study Group (EORTC/MSG).16 Disseminated disease was defined as a disease in two or more non-contiguous organs or bloodstream infection, while disease in adjacent organs was defined as IFI manifestation in two or more adjacent organs. fetched_contents.text: Invasive Trichoderma longibrachiatum infection in a neutropaenic patient 1. Introduction Trichoderma species are saprophytic filamentous fungi found in soil and decaying plant matter. They are a rare cause of human infection but can cause life-threatening disease in immunosuppressed patients with approximately 50 % mortality [1]. The few reports of Trichoderma infection in the literature are in patients with haematological malignancies and those requiring peritoneal dialysis with common sites of infection being lung and peritoneum [1]. In the absence of clinical breakpoints to interpret antifungal susceptibility testing or established clinical treatment guidelines, systemic antifungals such as amphotericin B or voriconazole are commonly used, in some cases combined with surgery. We present the case of invasive pulmonary infection with Trichoderma longibrachiatum in a neutropaenic patient being treated for acute myeloid leukaemia. 2. Case presentation A 51-year-old UK born female was electively admitted to a tertiary hospital in October 2023 (Day 0) for her first cycle of (Fla-Ida) (fludarabine, cytarabine (Ara-C), and idarubicin) chemotherapy for measurable-residual disease (MRD) positive acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). She had contracted SARS-CoV-2 1 month prior to admission and continued to test positive for SARS-CoV-2 during admission. She became neutropaenic on day 6 and on day 9 she developed neutropenic sepsis requiring a 4-day intensive care unit (ICU) admission for blood pressure support due to Enterobacter cloacae bacteraemia. Meropenem 1g TDS was started and continued throughout admission. On day 25 of her admission, she again developed neutropenic fevers [Fig. 1] while on meropenem and prophylactic itraconazole with temperatures up to 39.7 °C and an associated cough productive of brown sputum. On day 29 a high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of her chest was performed. This demonstrated multifocal consolidation and nodularity, many nodules being bronchocentric [Fig. 2]. There was also mediastinal stranding in keeping with mediastinitis and the tracheal wall was thickened. The following day serum β-D-glucan was positive at 360.4 pg/mL (Fungitell® assay, internally verified positive threshold of 110 pg/mL). Galactomannan was negative on days 30, 43 and 44. On day 29 prophylactic itraconazole was stopped and intravenous caspofungin 70mg once daily was started as per the protocol at our centre for suspected invasive fungal infection (IFI). Itraconazole drug trough levels had been satisfactory on day 30 at 0.84 mg/L. Intravenous catheter-related Enterococcus faecium and Staphyloccoccus epidermidis bacteraemias were identified on day 30 and lines were removed. Caspofungin was changed to intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome®) 3mg/kg once daily on day 34 due to persistent fevers >39 °C. Her fever and cough persisted despite this, and she developed intermittent chest pains, so a further HRCT was performed on day 41. This showed progressive consolidation within the lower lung lobe as well as scattered lung nodules and diffuse tracheal wall thickening [Fig. 3]. On the same day a mould was identified on Sabouraud agar from a sputum sample taken 9 days earlier. This was identified morphologically and by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation time-of-flight (MALDI-ToF) as Trichoderma longibrachiatum [Fig. 4]. T. longibrachiatum was isolated on a total of 4 sputum samples taken on days 32, 38, 48, and 55. Repeat serum β-D-glucans were considered equivocal (between 50 and 110 pg/mL) on day 42 (104 pg/mL), 43 (68 pg/mL) and 46 (93 pg/mL). The initial isolate was sent to the UK Health Security Agency National Mycology Reference Laboratory, where isolate identification was confirmed and antifungal susceptibility testing was performed using CLSI broth microdilution methodologies [2]. Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs), available on day 50, were as follows: amphotericin B 1.0 mg/L, caspofungin 0.03 mg/L, itraconazole 2 mg/L, posaconazole 0.5 mg/L and voriconazole 0.25 mg. In the absence of species-specific interpretive breakpoints for Trichoderma spp., MICs were interpreted against breakpoints developed for Aspergillus fumigatus, indicating likely susceptibility to amphotericin B, caspofungin and voriconazole, resistance to itraconazole and intermediate susceptibility to posaconazole. On day 48, due to persistent fevers despite liposomal amphotericin B, voriconazole 200mg twice daily was added as a second agent. Her fevers began to improve 48 hours following this addition, and she began to feel brighter and sit out of bed more. This was accompanied by a fall in C-reactive protein from 143 mg/L on day 47–88 mg/L on day 55. The patient's renal function deteriorated therefore amphotericin B was changed back to caspofungin and voriconazole was continued. Voriconazole trough levels were supratherapeutic at 14.4 mg/L and 5.5 mg/L on day 52 and 55 (target trough level 1 to <5.5mg/L). On day 54, the patient deteriorated clinically. She felt unable to expectorate and had an audible chest rattle. A repeat HRCT the following day showed stable appearances of the pulmonary nodules, however there was ulceration and perforation of the posterior wall of the trachea with surrounding emphysema. That evening the patient sustained a cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated. During intubation the trachea was found to be very oedematous, with blood-stained frothy secretions. After return of spontaneous circulation, she was transferred to the ICU. Bronchoscopy in the ICU demonstrated a lesion on the posterior wall of the trachea which was almost obstructing the entire lumen and thought to be an eroding fungal lesion. She later desaturated further, with heavily blood-stained secretions, suffering a further hypoxic cardiac arrest from which she did not recover. 3. However, the poor sensitivity and positive predictive value of some of these techniques in certain circumstances, and the potential delay in starting treatment due to logistical reasons, cause the management of IFIs to remain a challenge [1,4,5]. Core antifungal treatments for Trichoderma infections

The evidence base indicates that the most commonly used antifungal agents in reported Trichoderma infections are amphotericin B, voriconazole, and caspofungin, with additional mention of itraconazole, posaconazole, and terbinafine in broader antifungal discussions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1]. In the reviewed literature and the FungiScope® registry, 84% of 50 invasive Trichoderma cases received systemic antifungal therapy, mostly amphotericin B in 27 cases and voriconazole in 15 cases; caspofungin was also used in 7 cases [N3-F1]. A separate case series reported that amphotericin B, voriconazole, and caspofungin were the most commonly used agents, with amphotericin B noted as the most commonly used antifungal agent in the literature [N3-R2]. A 2022 review also states that Trichoderma isolates show relatively high MICs in vitro for other antifungal drugs, except for echinocandins and voriconazole [N3-F1]. This suggests that amphotericin B, voriconazole, and caspofungin are the most clinically prominent agents in reported cases, while other azoles appear to be less frequently cited as first-line choices in the Trichoderma-specific literature.

Dose, route, and duration of treatment are less clearly standardized in the evidence, but several sources provide partial guidance. The FungiScope® review notes that systemic antifungal therapy was administered, mostly amphotericin B (lipid-based formulation in 13 of 27 cases) and voriconazole in 15 cases [N3-F1]. It also reports that in one case series, liposomal amphotericin B was used at 3 mg/kg once daily, and voriconazole was added as a second agent at 200 mg twice daily [N3-F2]. In that case, amphotericin B was later changed to caspofungin when renal function deteriorated, and voriconazole was continued; voriconazole trough levels were supratherapeutic at 14.4 mg/L and 5.5 mg/L [N3-F2]. Although the evidence does not provide a single standard regimen, it suggests that amphotericin B is often given intravenously in lipid-based formulations, voriconazole intravenously at a typical 200 mg twice-daily dose, and caspofungin intravenously as a standard echinocandin dose [N3-F1][N3-F2].

Special considerations for immunocompromised or severe infections are especially important. The literature emphasizes that Trichoderma infections are life-threatening in immunocompromised patients, especially after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (HSCT) and solid-organ transplantation (SOT), where mortality was 80% in HSCT and 77% in SOT recipients [N3-F1]. In the FungiScope® review, overall mortality was 48% across all 50 cases, with the highest mortality in HSCT and SOT recipients [N3-F1]. The same source reports that surgical interventions were performed in 26% of cases and that mortality was 55% in amphotericin B-treated patients, 46% in voriconazole-treated patients, and 28% in caspofungin-treated patients [N3-F1]. The cited case series also describes a neutropaenic patient receiving prophylactic itraconazole and then switching to caspofungin before amphotericin B, followed by addition of voriconazole when persistent fever continued [N3-F2]. This pattern supports the idea that severe or immunocompromised infection often involves initial or bridging antifungal therapy, with escalation to a second agent if response is inadequate.

In broader clinical context, the evidence also notes that Trichoderma infections are mainly seen in patients with hematological malignancies and in continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) patients, with common infection sites in the lung and peritoneum [N3-F1]. The literature further reports that Trichoderma longibrachiatum infections can occur in neutropaenic patients, with the case described as an acute myeloid leukaemia patient undergoing chemotherapy and SARS-CoV-2 infection [N3-F2]. These findings support the need for targeted antifungal therapy in high-risk hemato-oncological and transplant patients, with close monitoring for drug interactions, toxicity, and response [N3-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also underscores that there are no evidence-based guidelines for Trichoderma infections, which makes the choice of agents and duration highly dependent on expert judgment and local practice [N3-F1].

Overall, the core antifungal treatments for Trichoderma infections in the evidence are amphotericin B, voriconazole, and caspofungin, with some support for itraconazole and posaconazole in broader antifungal discussions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1]. The evidence is strongest for intravenous use of amphotericin B and voriconazole, while caspofungin is used intravenously as well. In immunocompromised or severe infections, treatment often involves initial or bridging therapy, escalation when needed, and surgical intervention where appropriate [N3-F1][N3-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
Combination therapy approaches and rationale

The evidence for combination antifungal therapy in fungal infections is strongest for polyenes, azoles, and echinocandins, with the literature stating that the combination of polyenes or azoles with echinocandins suggests additive or synergistic effects in some preclinical studies [N2-R1]. Another source similarly notes that echinocandins and polyenes are not antagonistic and that echinocandins may provide additive to synergistic activity when combined with other agents [N2-R4]. A review of combination antifungal therapy also states that the concept is attractive because it offers the possibility of synergy or at least additivity [N2-R3]. Taken together, these sources support the rationale that combination therapy is used when the goal is to enhance efficacy, reduce resistance risk, or improve safety by reducing the burden of a single class of agent [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

The most directly supported combination approaches in the evidence include amphotericin B with azoles or echinocandins. The evidence specifically mentions that amphotericin B combined with itraconazole, amphotericin B plus a triazole, and voriconazole plus caspofungin showed synergy against dematiaceous fungi in in vitro studies [N1-R3]. A 2022 review of Trichoderma infections reports that three out of four patients treated with a combination of voriconazole and caspofungin survived [N3-R4]. This is a key example of a combination supported by reported clinical outcomes, even though it is still limited by small case numbers and lack of randomized trials [N3-F1][N3-R4]. The broader invasive fungal infection literature also supports changing antifungal class after prophylaxis failure, which is consistent with combination strategies when one agent is not sufficient [N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that azole prophylaxis may be an option in breakthrough filamentous fungal infection, but this is more relevant to prophylaxis than to combination therapy [N5-R1].

Mechanisms of synergy or reduced toxicity are partially explained in the evidence. Echinocandins inhibit fungal cell-wall synthesis and are not antagonistic with polyenes or azoles; they may provide additive or synergistic effects [N2-R1][N2-R4]. Amphotericin B, which is a polyene, can cause nephrotoxicity, so combination with echinocandins or azoles may reduce the dose or duration of amphotericin B needed, thereby lowering toxicity [N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that voriconazole and caspofungin were combined in a reported case series and that three of four patients survived [N3-R4]. While this does not provide a direct mechanistic explanation, it is consistent with the broader rationale that combination therapy can improve clinical response when a single agent is insufficient [N2-R3][N3-R4].

Clinical settings where combination therapy is preferred are not fully standardized for Trichoderma, but the evidence suggests it is most relevant for severe or refractory infections. Invasive Trichoderma infections are described as life-threatening, especially in HSCT and SOT recipients, and the literature reports that mortality was 80% in HSCT and 77% in SOT recipients [N3-F1]. The case series also describes a patient who required a change from itraconazole to caspofungin and then to amphotericin B, followed by addition of voriconazole when persistent fever continued [N3-F2]. This pattern supports the use of combination therapy when initial monotherapy is inadequate. The broader invasive fungal infection literature also notes that a high percentage of clinicians change antifungal class after failure of prophylaxis, which is consistent with combination therapy when one agent fails [N5-F3]. Thus, combination therapy is especially preferred in severe, refractory, or immunocompromised infections where monotherapy may not be sufficient [N2-R3][N3-F1][N5-F3].

In summary, the evidence supports combination approaches involving amphotericin B with azoles or echinocandins, and voriconazole with caspofungin [N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4][N3-R4]. The rationale includes additive or synergistic effects, reduced toxicity, and improved clinical response, especially in severe or immunocompromised infections [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence is strongest for these combinations in broader fungal infection guidance and weaker in Trichoderma-specific clinical trials [N1-R3][N3-R4].

Clinical context and practical limitations

The clinical context for Trichoderma infections is dominated by immunocompromised patients, particularly those with hematological malignancies and those undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD), with lung and peritoneum as the most common infection sites [N3-F1]. The literature also reports that Trichoderma infections can occur in neutropaenic patients, including those with acute myeloid leukaemia undergoing chemotherapy [N3-F2]. Invasive Trichoderma infections are described as life-threatening complications, especially after HSCT and SOT, where mortality was 80% in HSCT and 77% in SOT recipients [N3-F1]. The same source reports overall mortality of 48% across 50 invasive cases, with the highest mortality in HSCT and SOT recipients [N3-F1]. This underscores that Trichoderma infections are most commonly treated in high-risk hemato-oncological and transplant populations, where the infection is often severe and mortality is substantial [N3-F1][N3-F2].

Drug availability, cost, and safety concerns are important practical limitations. The evidence highlights that amphotericin B is often used in lipid-based formulations, which are more tolerable than conventional amphotericin B but still costly and require careful monitoring for nephrotoxicity [N3-F1][N3-F2]. Voriconazole is typically administered intravenously at a standard dose of 200 mg twice daily in the case series [N3-F2], and it is associated with drug interactions that make routine therapeutic drug monitoring useful [N1-R4]. Caspofungin is another echinocandin used in the reviewed cases [N3-F1], and the broader antifungal literature notes that echinocandins have a favorable safety profile compared to polyenes, though they are not without cost and monitoring requirements [N2-R4][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that Trichoderma infections are rare and that treatment decisions are often made in the absence of species-specific clinical breakpoints or established guidelines [N3-F1][N3-R2]. This makes drug selection and dosing highly dependent on local practice, institutional protocols, and clinical judgment [N3-F1][N3-F2].

Gaps in evidence and areas needing more research are substantial. The literature explicitly states that there are no evidence-based guidelines for Trichoderma infections [N3-F1]. It also notes that clinical trials involving Trichoderma human infection are unlikely due to the paucity of cases [N3-R3]. In addition, the FungiScope® review reports that only 50 invasive infections were identified across the literature and registry, and that the mortality rate is reported to be as high as 53% [N3-F1]. The evidence further notes that Trichoderma isolates show relatively high MICs in vitro for other antifungal drugs, except for echinocandins and voriconazole, which suggests that susceptibility testing may not always guide treatment [N3-F1]. These limitations point to major gaps in evidence: small case numbers, lack of randomized trials, limited susceptibility data, and no established guidelines [N3-F1][N3-R3][N3-F2]. The broader invasive fungal infection literature also emphasizes that diagnostic and therapeutic strategies remain challenging, especially because of the poor sensitivity and positive predictive value of some tests and logistical delays [N5-F3]. For Trichoderma, these limitations mean that treatment decisions are often based on expert opinion and clinical experience rather than robust trial data [N3-F1][N3-R3].

In conclusion, Trichoderma infections are primarily treated in immunocompromised patients with hematological malignancies and CAPD, with the most common sites being lung and peritoneum [N3-F1]. Amphotericin B, voriconazole, and caspofungin are the main agents, but availability, cost, and safety concerns are important practical limitations [N3-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence base is weak, with no evidence-based guidelines and very few clinical trials, which leaves much room for further research on optimal regimens, susceptibility testing, and management strategies [N3-F1][N3-R3][N3-F2].

Trichoderma-specific treatment patterns and evidence gaps

Reported treatment regimens and survival outcomes show a pattern of systemic antifungal therapy, often combined with surgical intervention. In the reviewed literature and FungiScope® registry, 84% of 50 invasive Trichoderma cases received systemic antifungal therapy, mostly amphotericin B and voriconazole, with caspofungin also used in some cases [N3-F1]. The same source reports that surgical interventions were performed in 26% of cases and that mortality was 55% in amphotericin B-treated patients, 46% in voriconazole-treated patients, and 28% in caspofungin-treated patients [N3-F1]. A separate case series reported that three out of four patients treated with a combination of voriconazole and caspofungin survived [N3-R4]. This combination is especially noteworthy because it is one of the few reported regimens with survival data. The cited case series also describes a neutropaenic patient who received prophylactic itraconazole, then caspofungin, then amphotericin B, and finally voriconazole when persistent fever continued [N3-F2]. This sequence reflects a common clinical pattern in severe immunocompromised infection: initial or bridging therapy, escalation when needed, and addition of a second agent if response is inadequate [N3-F1][N3-F2].

The literature says that optimal combinations are not fully established. The evidence does support voriconazole plus caspofungin as one combination with reported survival benefit, but it is still limited by the small case series and lack of randomized trials [N3-R4]. The broader antifungal literature also supports combination approaches with polyenes, azoles, or echinocandins, suggesting that additive or synergistic effects may justify combination therapy [N1-R3][N2-R1]. However, the Trichoderma-specific evidence is not strong enough to define an optimal combination regimen. The literature further states that there are no evidence-based guidelines for Trichoderma infections [N3-F1], which means that recommendations are often based on expert judgment rather than rigorous trial data [N3-F1][N3-F2].

Limitations of case reports and lack of clinical trials are substantial. The evidence explicitly states that clinical trials involving Trichoderma human infection are unlikely due to the paucity of cases [N3-R3]. It also notes that Trichoderma infections are rare and that treatment decisions are often made in the absence of species-specific clinical breakpoints or established guidelines [N3-F1][N3-R2]. In addition, the FungiScope® review reports that only 50 invasive infections were identified across the literature and registry, and that the mortality rate is reported to be as high as 53% [N3-F1]. These limitations indicate that case reports are the primary source of evidence, but they are inherently limited by selection bias, small sample size, and the inability to establish causality or efficacy [N3-R3][N3-F1]. The broader invasive fungal infection literature also emphasizes that diagnostic and therapeutic strategies remain challenging, especially because of poor sensitivity and positive predictive value of some tests and logistical delays [N5-F3]. For Trichoderma, this means that reported treatment patterns should be interpreted cautiously and that they do not substitute for well-designed clinical trials [N3-R3][N3-F1][N3-F2].

Overall, the reported treatment patterns for Trichoderma infections include systemic antifungal therapy, often with amphotericin B, voriconazole, or caspofungin, and sometimes with surgical intervention [N3-F1][N3-F2]. Voriconazole plus caspofungin is one reported combination with survival benefit, but the evidence is still limited to case reports and small series [N3-R4]. The main evidence gaps are the lack of clinical trials, the absence of evidence-based guidelines, and the small number of reported cases, which severely limits the ability to determine optimal regimens [N3-F1][N3-R3][N3-F2].

# Commonly used antifungal treatments for infections caused by Trichoderma spp.

## 1) Most commonly used antifungal agents in reported Trichoderma infections

The evidence indicates that the most commonly used antifungal agents in reported Trichoderma infections are **amphotericin B**, **voriconazole**, and **caspofungin**, with additional mention of **itraconazole**, **posaconazole**, and **terbinafine** in broader antifungal discussions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1]. In the reviewed literature and the FungiScope® registry, 84% of 50 invasive Trichoderma cases received systemic antifungal therapy, mostly **amphotericin B** in 27 cases and **voriconazole** in 15 cases; **caspofungin** was also used in 7 cases [N3-F1]. A separate case series reported that **amphotericin B** was the most commonly used antifungal agent in the literature, while **voriconazole** and **caspofungin** were also frequently used [N3-R2]. A 2022 review further states that Trichoderma isolates show relatively high MICs in vitro for other antifungal drugs, except for **echinocandins** and **voriconazole** [N3-F1].

So, the core treatment choices for Trichoderma infections in reported cases are:

- **Amphotericin B**  
- **Voriconazole**  
- **Caspofungin**  
- **Itraconazole** and **posaconazole** as additional agents mentioned in broader antifungal discussions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1]

## 2) Dose, route, and duration of treatment for each agent

The evidence is not fully standardized, but several sources provide partial guidance on dosing and route:

- **Amphotericin B**: the reviewed literature notes that systemic antifungal therapy was administered, mostly in lipid-based formulations [N3-F1]. In one case series, **liposomal amphotericin B** was used at **3 mg/kg once daily** [N3-F2]. - **Voriconazole**: the same case series reports that **voriconazole** was added as a second agent at **200 mg twice daily** [N3-F2]. It is also associated with drug interactions that make routine therapeutic drug monitoring useful [N1-R4].

## 5) Clinical context and practical limitations

The clinical context for Trichoderma infections is dominated by **immunocompromised patients**, particularly those with **hematological malignancies** and those undergoing **CAPD**, with **lung** and **peritoneum** as the most common infection sites [N3-F1]. The clinical context for Trichoderma infections is dominated by immunocompromised patients, particularly those with hematological malignancies and those undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD), with lung and peritoneum as the most common infection sites [N3-F1]. The literature also reports that Trichoderma infections can occur in neutropaenic patients, including those with acute myeloid leukaemia undergoing chemotherapy [N3-F2]. Invasive Trichoderma infections are described as life-threatening complications, especially after HSCT and SOT, where mortality was 80% in HSCT and 77% in SOT recipients [N3-F1]. The same source reports overall mortality of 48% across 50 invasive cases, with the highest mortality in HSCT and SOT recipients [N3-F1]. This underscores that Trichoderma infections are most commonly treated in high-risk hemato-oncological and transplant populations, where the infection is often severe and mortality is substantial [N3-F1][N3-F2].

Drug availability, cost, and safety concerns are important practical limitations. The evidence highlights that amphotericin B is often used in lipid-based formulations, which are more tolerable than conventional amphotericin B but still costly and require careful monitoring for nephrotoxicity [N3-F1][N3-F2]. Voriconazole is typically administered intravenously at a standard dose of 200 mg twice daily in the case series [N3-F2], and it is associated with drug interactions that make routine therapeutic drug monitoring useful [N1-R4]. Caspofungin is another echinocandin used in the reviewed cases [N3-F1], and the broader antifungal literature notes that echinocandins have a favorable safety profile compared to polyenes, though they are not without cost and monitoring requirements [N2-R4][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that Trichoderma infections are rare and that treatment decisions are often made in the absence of species-specific clinical breakpoints or established guidelines [N3-F1][N3-R2]. This makes drug selection and dosing highly dependent on local practice, institutional protocols, and clinical judgment [N3-F1][N3-F2].

Gaps in evidence and areas needing more research are substantial. The literature explicitly states that there are no evidence-based guidelines for Trichoderma infections [N3-F1]. It also notes that clinical trials involving Trichoderma human infection are unlikely due to the paucity of cases [N3-R3]. In addition, the FungiScope® review reports that only 50 invasive infections were identified across the literature and registry, and that the mortality rate is reported to be as high as 53% [N3-F1]. The evidence further notes that Trichoderma isolates show relatively high MICs in vitro for other antifungal drugs, except for echinocandins and voriconazole, which suggests that susceptibility testing may not always guide treatment [N3-F1]. These limitations point to major gaps in evidence: small case numbers, lack of randomized trials, limited susceptibility data, and no established guidelines [N3-F1][N3-R3][N3-F2]. The broader invasive fungal infection literature also emphasizes that diagnostic and therapeutic strategies remain challenging, especially because of the poor sensitivity and positive predictive value of some tests and logistical delays [N5-F3]. For Trichoderma, these limitations mean that treatment decisions are often based on expert opinion and clinical experience rather than robust trial data [N3-F1][N3-R3].

In conclusion, Trichoderma infections are primarily treated in immunocompromised patients with hematological malignancies and CAPD, with the most common sites being lung and peritoneum [N3-F1]. Amphotericin B, voriconazole, and caspofungin are the main agents, but availability, cost, and safety concerns are important practical limitations [N3-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence base is weak, with no evidence-based guidelines and very few clinical trials, which leaves much room for further research on optimal regimens, susceptibility testing, and management strategies [N3-F1][N3-R3][N3-F2].

# Commonly used antifungal treatments for infections caused by Trichoderma spp.

## 1) Most commonly used antifungal agents in reported Trichoderma infections

The evidence indicates that the most commonly used antifungal agents in reported Trichoderma infections are **amphotericin B**, **voriconazole**, and **caspofungin**, with additional mention of **itraconazole**, **posaconazole**, and **terbinafine** in broader antifungal discussions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1]. In the reviewed literature and the FungiScope® registry, 84% of 50 invasive Trichoderma cases received systemic antifungal therapy, mostly **amphotericin B** in 27 cases and **voriconazole** in 15 cases; **caspofungin** was also used in 7 cases [N3-F1]. A separate case series reported that **amphotericin B** was the most commonly used antifungal agent in the literature, while **voriconazole** and **caspofungin** were also frequently used [N3-R2]. A 2022 review further states that Trichoderma isolates show relatively high MICs in vitro for other antifungal drugs, except for **echinocandins** and **voriconazole** [N3-F1].

So, the core treatment choices for Trichoderma infections in reported cases are:

- **Amphotericin B**  
- **Voriconazole**  
- **Caspofungin**  
- **Itraconazole** and **posaconazole** as additional agents mentioned in broader antifungal discussions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1]

## 2) Dose, route, and duration of treatment for each agent

The evidence is not fully standardized, but several sources provide partial guidance on dosing and route:

- **Amphotericin B**: the reviewed literature notes that systemic antifungal therapy was administered, mostly in lipid-based formulations [N3-F1]. In one case series, **liposomal amphotericin B** was used at **3 mg/kg once daily** [N3-F2]. The evidence also mentions that amphotericin B may be used in the absence of species-specific clinical breakpoints, and that treatment decisions are often made in the absence of established guidelines [N3-F1][N3-F2].

- **Voriconazole**: the same case series reports that **voriconazole** was added as a second agent at **200 mg twice daily** [N3-F2]. It is also associated with drug interactions that make routine therapeutic drug monitoring useful [N1-R4].

- **Caspofungin**: the reviewed literature reports that **caspofungin** was used in 7 cases [N3-F1], and the broader antifungal literature describes it as an echinocandin with a favorable safety profile [N2-R4][N5-F3]. Although the evidence does not provide a standard regimen, it is consistent with intravenous use for severe infections [N3-F1][N3-F2].

- **Itraconazole and posaconazole**: these are mentioned in broader antifungal discussions but are not as prominently cited in the Trichoderma-specific literature as amphotericin B, voriconazole, and caspofungin [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1].

Duration of treatment is not clearly standardized in the evidence, but the clinical context strongly suggests prolonged or escalation-based therapy. In one case series, treatment was adjusted over time: prophylactic **itraconazole** was stopped, **caspofungin** was started, then **amphotericin B** was added, and finally **voriconazole** was added when persistent fever continued [N3-F2]. This pattern reflects the need for escalation in severe or refractory cases.

## 3) Special considerations for immunocompromised or severe infections

Trichoderma infections are especially dangerous in **immunocompromised patients**, particularly those with **hematological malignancies** and those undergoing **continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD)**, with common infection sites in the **lung** and **peritoneum** [N3-F1]. The literature reports that invasive Trichoderma infections are life-threatening complications, especially after **hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (HSCT)** and **solid-organ transplantation (SOT)**, where mortality was **80% in HSCT recipients** and **77% in SOT recipients** [N3-F1]. Overall mortality across 50 invasive cases was **48%**, with the highest mortality in HSCT and SOT recipients [N3-F1].

In immunocompromised or severe infections, the evidence supports:

- **Initial or bridging antifungal therapy**, with escalation when response is inadequate [N3-F1][N3-F2].
- **Surgical intervention** where appropriate, as surgical interventions were performed in 26% of cases [N3-F1].
- **Close monitoring for drug interactions, toxicity, and response**, especially with voriconazole and amphotericin B [N1-R4][N3-F2].

The absence of evidence-based guidelines for Trichoderma infections means that treatment decisions are highly dependent on expert judgment and local practice [N3-F1].

## 4) Combination therapy approaches and rationale

Combination antifungal therapy is supported in broader fungal infection guidance for **polyenes**, **azoles**, and **echinocandins**, with the literature stating that the combination of polyenes or azoles with echinocandins suggests **additive or synergistic effects** in some preclinical studies [N2-R1]. Another source similarly notes that **echinocandins and polyenes are not antagonistic** and may provide **additive to synergistic activity** when combined with other agents [N2-R4]. A review of combination antifungal therapy also states that the concept is attractive because it offers the possibility of **synergy or at least additivity** [N2-R3].

The evidence specifically supports several combinations:

- **Amphotericin B with itraconazole or amphotericin B plus a triazole**  
- **Amphotericin B with voriconazole**  
- **Voriconazole plus caspofungin** [N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4]

Mechanisms of synergy or reduced toxicity include:

- **Additive or synergistic effects** when polyenes, azoles, or echinocandins are combined [N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Reduced toxicity** by lowering the dose or duration of amphotericin B [N2-R4].
- **Improved clinical response** when a single agent is insufficient [N2-R3][N3-R4].

## 6) Trichoderma-specific treatment patterns and evidence gaps

Reported treatment patterns show a pattern of **systemic antifungal therapy**, often combined with **surgical intervention**. In the reviewed literature and FungiScope® registry, 84% of 50 invasive Trichoderma cases received systemic antifungal therapy, mostly **amphotericin B** and **voriconazole**, with **caspofungin** also used in some cases [N3-F1]. Surgical interventions were performed in 26% of cases, and mortality was 55% in amphotericin B-treated patients, 46% in voriconazole-treated patients, and 28% in caspofungin-treated patients [N3-F1]. A separate case series reported that **three out of four patients treated with a combination of voriconazole and caspofungin survived** [N3-R4].

The literature says that **optimal combinations are not fully established**. The evidence does support **voriconazole plus caspofungin** as one combination with reported survival benefit, but it is still limited by the small case series and lack of randomized trials [N3-R4]. The broader antifungal literature also supports combination approaches with polyenes, azoles, or echinocandins, suggesting that additive or synergistic effects may justify combination therapy [N1-R3][N2-R1]. However, the Trichoderma-specific evidence is not strong enough to define an optimal combination regimen [N3-F1].

Limitations of case reports and lack of clinical trials are substantial. The evidence explicitly states that **clinical trials involving Trichoderma human infection are unlikely due to the paucity of cases** [N3-R3]. It also notes that Trichoderma infections are rare and that treatment decisions are often made in the absence of species-specific clinical breakpoints or established guidelines [N3-F1][N3-R2]. In addition, the FungiScope® review reports that only 50 invasive infections were identified across the literature and registry, and that the mortality rate is reported to be as high as **53%** [N3-F1]. These limitations indicate that case reports are the primary source of evidence, but they are inherently limited by selection bias, small sample size, and the inability to establish causality or efficacy [N3-R3][N3-F1].

## 7) Bottom line

In clinical practice, the commonly used antifungal treatments for infections caused by **Trichoderma spp.** are:

- **Amphotericin B**  
- **Voriconazole**  
- **Caspofungin**  
- **Itraconazole** and **posaconazole** as additional agents mentioned in broader antifungal discussions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1]

**Combination therapies** supported by evidence or expert opinion include:

- **Amphotericin B with itraconazole or a triazole**  
- **Amphotericin B with voriconazole**  
- **Voriconazole plus caspofungin** [N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4][N3-R4]

**Special considerations** are especially important in **immunocompromised or severe infections**, where treatment often involves **initial or bridging therapy, escalation when needed, and surgical intervention** [N3-F1][N3-F2]. The literature also emphasizes that **there are no evidence-based guidelines** for Trichoderma infections [N3-F1], and that **clinical trials are unlikely due to the paucity of cases** [N3-R3].

## 8) Conclusion

Overall, the evidence suggests that **amphotericin B**, **voriconazole**, and **caspofungin** are the most commonly used antifungal treatments for Trichoderma infections in reported cases, with **combination therapy** being especially relevant in severe or refractory disease [N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F1][N3-R4]. However, the evidence base remains weak, and treatment decisions are still largely guided by **expert judgment**, **clinical experience**, and **local protocols** rather than robust randomized trials [N3-F1][N3-R3].
